title: From Hunting to Farming
bigQuestion: Why did people who had hunted and gathered for tens of thousands of years start to farm, and what did that choice cost them?

story.title: The Autumn Some of Them Stayed
story.kicker: For a thousand generations a band followed the herds. Then, in one river valley, a few families put down their packs and did not pick them up again.
paragraphs: Picture a band of about thirty people walking a ridge in the hills that we now call the Fertile Crescent, roughly eleven thousand years ago. They carry everything they own: hide packs, spear throwers, baskets, a baby or two. They are following the gazelle herds down toward the winter grass, the way their grandparents did. No one in the band has ever slept in the same camp for a whole year.

This valley is different. A spring bubbles from the rock, and along the stream grow thick stands of wild wheat and barley. In early summer the grass heads turn gold and the seeds fall. Two young women, cousins, have been coming here every year with their stone-bladed sickles. They can cut enough grain in three weeks to fill dozens of baskets. This year they stored it in a pit lined with clay, and the mice did not get it.

When the band gathers to leave, the cousins say they will stay. There is grain in the pit, nuts on the trees, fish in the stream. They will build a hut with stone footings and a reed roof. A few others agree, including an old man whose knees hurt and a hunter who has noticed that the gazelles keep coming back to this same water. The rest of the band shakes their heads and walks on toward the lowlands.

Spring comes. Where the cousins spilled grain near the hut, new wheat comes up in a green tangle. They notice something odd. In the wild patches, ripe seeds scatter the moment you touch them. The plants near the hut hold their seeds tighter, because those were the seeds that stayed on the stalk long enough to be carried home. Without planning it, the cousins have started to choose the grain they will live on.

Ten years later the hut is a cluster of huts. The pit is a row of storage rooms. The people who stayed have more children than the people who walked on, but they also have more toothaches, more sore backs and their first serious quarrel over who owns the best patch of ground. Archaeologists can dig up the houses, the sickle blades and the grain. The quarrel they can only guess at.
story.think: The cousins gained a full storehouse and a permanent home. What do you think they gave up? Would you have stayed or walked on?

lessons.title: History Without Writing
lessons.mainIdea: For almost all of human time there was no writing, so we learn about early people from the objects and traces they left behind.
reading: Modern humans have lived on Earth for at least two hundred thousand years. Writing is only about five thousand years old. That means more than ninety-five percent of the human story happened before anyone could write it down. Historians call this long stretch *prehistory*, meaning the time before written records. It is not a time without history. It is a time we have to read in a different way.

The people who read it are called *archaeologists*. They study the physical remains of past people: stone tools, animal bones, ash from fires, seeds, house foundations, paintings on cave walls, and the graves where people buried their dead. Every scrap is a clue. A pile of cracked bones near a hearth tells you what people ate and that they cooked it. A bead made of shell found three hundred miles from the sea tells you people traded or traveled.

An archaeological *site* is any place where these remains are found. Some sites are caves that people lived in for thousands of years. Others are open camps by old lakeshores, or mounds where a village stood. In Illinois, archaeologists have found spear points and camps along the rivers that are more than ten thousand years old. The ground under a cornfield can hold a whole chapter of the past.

The hardest part of prehistory is that objects do not explain themselves. A carved figure might be a toy, a god or a good-luck charm. Archaeologists build arguments from evidence, and they change their minds when new evidence turns up. That is what makes the field honest: the answer is always only as good as the digging behind it.

words.d: the very long time before people invented writing
a scientist who studies past people through the objects and traces they left behind
a place where remains of past people are found and studied

look.title: A Camp by a Dry Lake
look.text: Imagine a team digs a camp on the edge of a long-dried lake. They find hundreds of fish bones, a few charred acorn shells, a broken spear point, and a small pit with three burned stones inside. There are no walls and no graves.
look.prompt: What can you say for certain about the people who camped here? What would you only be guessing?

check.q: What does the word prehistory mean?
choices: The time before people invented writing
The time before people existed
A history that turned out to be false
The history of ancient Greece and Rome
check.why: Prehistory is the long period before written records. People lived, worked and built during it, but nobody could write about it.

check.q: A shell bead is found far inland, hundreds of miles from any sea. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The sea once covered that spot
People traded or traveled long distances
The bead was made of stone, not shell
Someone lost it last year
check.why: A shell object far from the coast is evidence that people moved things across long distances, by trade or travel.

check.q: Why do archaeologists sometimes change their conclusions?
choices: They are not allowed to publish old ideas
Objects from the past rot within a few years
New evidence can show that an old argument was wrong
Writing from prehistory is often mistranslated
check.why: Archaeologists argue from evidence. When new digging turns up new evidence, the argument has to change with it.

lessons.title: Tools, Bones and Layers
lessons.mainIdea: Stone tools, bones and the order of layers in the ground let archaeologists tell what early people did and roughly when.
reading: Stone lasts. Wood, leather and cloth rot away, but a flint blade knapped fifty thousand years ago is still sharp today. That is why the earliest ages of human life are named for tools. The *Paleolithic*, or Old Stone Age, covers the long time when people chipped stone into hand axes, scrapers and points. Later people learned to grind and polish stone into smooth axes, and archaeologists call that the Neolithic, or New Stone Age, the age when farming began.

Bones talk too. The bones of hunted animals show cut marks where stone blades sliced off meat. Human bones show how tall people were, how hard they worked and what diseases they had. In 1991 hikers in the Alps found a man frozen in the ice with his clothes, copper axe and a quiver of arrows. Scientists nicknamed him Ötzi. He died about fifty-three hundred years ago, and his body showed an arrow wound in his shoulder and worn joints from years of walking hills.

To find out how old something is, archaeologists first look at where it lies. Dirt builds up over time, so deeper layers are usually older. This rule is called *stratigraphy*, from a word meaning layers. A tool found under a layer of volcanic ash is older than the eruption that dropped the ash. Reading the layers is like reading the pages of a book from the bottom up.

For real dates, scientists use *radiocarbon dating*. Living things take in a rare form of carbon that slowly breaks down after death at a known rate. By measuring how much is left in a bone, a seed or a piece of charcoal, a lab can estimate its age back to about fifty thousand years. The method was invented in the late 1940s by the American chemist Willard Libby. It changed prehistory from guesswork into a timeline.

words.d: the Old Stone Age, the long time when people made tools by chipping stone
reading the layers of the ground; deeper layers are usually older
a lab method that estimates the age of once-living material from the carbon left in it

look.title: How Old Are These Finds?
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Chauvet paintings and the first writing? What does that gap tell you about how much of the human story is prehistory?

check.q: Why are the earliest ages of human life named after stone tools?
choices: Early people used nothing but stone
Stone was the most valuable material
Ancient writers chose those names
Stone survives while wood, leather and cloth rot away
check.why: Stone tools last for tens of thousands of years, so they are the evidence that survives best from the earliest times.

check.q: A stone point is found in a layer below a layer of volcanic ash. What can you conclude?
choices: The point is older than the eruption
The point is younger than the eruption
The point was made from the ash
The eruption and the point happened the same year
check.why: Layers build up over time. Something below the ash was there before the ash fell.

check.q: What does radiocarbon dating measure?
choices: The weight of a stone tool
How much of a rare form of carbon is left in once-living material
The depth of a layer of soil
The number of cut marks on a bone
check.why: Living things take in a rare carbon that decays at a known rate after death, so the amount left tells the age.

lessons.title: Paintings in the Dark
lessons.mainIdea: Cave paintings show that Ice Age people had skill, imagination and beliefs, even though we cannot be sure what the pictures meant.
reading: In September of 1940, four teenagers near the village of Lascaux in southern France followed their dog into a hole in the ground. They found themselves in a cave whose walls were covered with painted animals: horses, bulls, deer and a strange spotted creature with two straight horns. Some of the bulls are more than fifteen feet long. The paintings were made about seventeen thousand years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age.

The painters worked deep underground by the light of small lamps burning animal fat. They ground colored earth and charcoal into powder and mixed it with water or fat. They used brushes of hair, pads of moss and even blew paint through hollow bones to make a spray. They used the bumps of the rock to make a horse's shoulder swell out. These were not clumsy scratches. They were the work of trained artists.

Lascaux is not alone. Chauvet Cave, also in France, holds paintings of lions, rhinos and bears that are about twice as old. In Spain, Indonesia and Australia, other caves hold hands stenciled onto the rock and animals drawn in red ochre. Wherever people lived in the Ice Age, some of them made *cave art*.

What did it mean? No one knows for certain. Some scholars think the paintings were hunting magic, made to bring the herds. Others think the caves were places for ceremonies, or that the animals were spirits, or that the art recorded stories. Almost no pictures show plants, and very few show people. Whatever the reason, the caves prove one thing: people thirty thousand years ago had minds as full and curious as our own.

words.d: paintings and carvings made on cave walls by people in the Ice Age
a natural colored earth, often red or yellow, used as paint

look.title: Standing in Lascaux
look.text: You crouch through a low passage with a flickering fat lamp. The ceiling opens into a hall, and painted bulls seem to run around the walls in the moving light. Your lamp will burn for maybe an hour. The nearest daylight is far behind you.
look.prompt: Why would people go to so much trouble to paint in a place that was dark, cold and hard to reach? What does the location itself suggest?

check.q: How were the paintings at Lascaux discovered?
choices: Archaeologists dug into a hillside on purpose
A farmer plowed up a painted stone
Teenagers followed their dog into a hole
Miners broke into the cave by accident
check.why: In 1940 four teenagers near Lascaux, France, followed their dog into a hole and found the painted cave.

check.q: Which statement about the meaning of cave art is most accurate?
choices: The paintings were certainly hunting magic
The paintings were signed and dated by the artists
The paintings were mostly of plants and people
Scholars have several ideas, but no one is certain
check.why: The reading offers several possible meanings and says no one knows for certain. The evidence does not settle it.

check.q: What does the skill in the paintings tell us about Ice Age people?
choices: They had trained artists with real technique and imagination
They could not make tools
They spent most of their time underground
They lived in cities
check.why: Using lamps, brushes, sprayed paint and the shape of the rock shows practice and planning, not clumsy scratching.

lessons.title: Skills of a Foraging Band
lessons.mainIdea: Hunter-gatherers lived in small mobile bands and survived through deep knowledge of plants, animals and each other.
reading: For most of prehistory, every person on Earth was a *hunter-gatherer*. People hunted animals, fished and gathered wild plants, nuts, eggs and honey. They did not plant crops or keep herds. They lived in small groups, called *bands*, usually of twenty to fifty people who were related by blood or marriage. When the food in one place ran low, the band moved to the next.

This life took enormous knowledge. A gatherer had to know hundreds of plants: which roots were safe, which berries were poison, when each ripened. A hunter had to read tracks, know the wind, and understand the habits of every animal. People made spears, bows, nets, traps, baskets, needles from bone, and rope from plant fibers. They knew how to make fire and how to cook a poisonous plant until it was safe. In many bands, plants gathered by women provided more of the daily food than hunting did.

Bands shared. When a hunter killed a deer, everyone ate. This was not just kindness; it was insurance. A hunter fails most days, so sharing meant no family went hungry for long. Studies of hunter-gatherers who still lived this way in the twentieth century found that many worked fewer hours to feed themselves than farmers did. They had little property because everything had to be carried.

There were no kings and no rich families. Leaders were people others chose to listen to, and a leader who bossed people around could simply be ignored. Life was not easy. Injuries, hunger in bad seasons and childhood illness were common, and few people lived to old age. But it was a way of life that worked for two hundred thousand years.

words.d: a person who lives by hunting animals and gathering wild plants rather than farming
a small group of related people, usually twenty to fifty, who live and move together
to search for and collect wild food

look.title: A Week's Food
look.text: In one band, the hunters bring back a wild pig on Monday and nothing for the next five days. Every day the gatherers return with baskets of tubers, greens, nuts and a few birds' eggs. On Sunday a boy finds a bee tree.
look.prompt: Which food was more dependable? Why might a band that shared everything do better than one where each family kept what it found?

check.q: About how big was a typical hunter-gatherer band?
choices: Two or three people
Twenty to fifty people
Several hundred people
Thousands of people
check.why: Bands were small, usually twenty to fifty related people, small enough to move together and feed themselves.

check.q: Why did bands share food so widely?
choices: Their leaders ordered them to
Meat could be stored for years
Hunting often failed, so sharing kept everyone fed
They had no way to cook food alone
check.why: A hunter fails most days. Sharing meant that when anyone succeeded, no one went hungry.

check.q: Why did hunter-gatherers own so little property?
choices: They were forbidden to own things
They had no tools or clothing
They did not know how to make objects
Everything they owned had to be carried when they moved
check.why: Bands moved often, so people kept only what they could carry.

lessons.title: The Ice Age World
lessons.mainIdea: During the last Ice Age, huge ice sheets covered much of the north, sea levels fell, and people adapted to a cold world full of giant animals.
reading: About twenty thousand years ago the Earth was in the coldest stretch of the last *Ice Age*. Sheets of ice a mile thick covered Canada and reached south into what is now Illinois. The ice scraped the land flat and left behind the rich soil that Illinois farmers plow today. So much water was locked in ice that the oceans were roughly four hundred feet lower than now. Coastlines stretched far out, and land bridges connected places that are islands today.

South of the ice lay cold, dry grasslands. On them grazed animals that are now gone: woolly mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, and bison much bigger than today's. Hunters followed these herds. A single mammoth could feed a band for weeks. People used the bones for tools and, in places with no trees, built huts out of mammoth bones and tusks covered with hides.

Surviving the cold took invention. People sewed fitted clothing with bone needles, built warm shelters, and kept fires burning through long winters. They made spear throwers, a short stick that let a hunter hurl a spear farther and harder. They stored meat in cold pits. Living through the Ice Age was one of the hardest things humans have ever done.

Then the world warmed. Between about fifteen thousand and ten thousand years ago the ice melted back, seas rose and flooded the land bridges, and forests spread north over the old grasslands. Many of the giant animals died out, from the changing climate, from hunting, or both. People had to find new ways to live. That challenge is part of why farming began when it did.

words.d: a long cold period when ice sheets covered large parts of the Earth
dry land that connects two regions when sea levels are low
a large, hairy relative of the elephant that lived in the Ice Age

look.title: Ice Over Illinois
look.text: Stand in a flat Illinois cornfield and imagine a wall of ice, taller than any building in Chicago, stretching to the northern horizon. As it melted it dropped the ground-up rock and dust that became some of the deepest topsoil on Earth.
look.prompt: How could something as destructive as a mile-thick sheet of ice end up being a gift to farmers thousands of years later?

check.q: Why were sea levels much lower during the Ice Age?
choices: A great deal of ocean water was locked up in ice sheets
The oceans had not formed yet
Rivers flowed backward into the mountains
The Earth was smaller
check.why: Water that fell as snow stayed frozen in giant ice sheets instead of returning to the sea, so the oceans dropped.

check.q: Which of these did Ice Age people use to survive the cold?
choices: Coal furnaces
Fitted clothing sewn with bone needles
Brick houses with glass windows
Wool from farm sheep
check.why: Ice Age hunters had no farm animals or bricks, but they did sew warm fitted clothing with bone needles.

check.q: What happened to the land bridges when the Ice Age ended?
choices: They rose higher above the sea
They turned into deserts
Rising seas flooded them
They were covered by new ice
check.why: As the ice melted, the water returned to the oceans, and the seas rose over the low land bridges.

lessons.title: Peopling the Continents
lessons.mainIdea: Modern humans spread from Africa across every continent except Antarctica, reaching the Americas near the end of the Ice Age.
reading: Modern humans first appeared in Africa. The oldest fossils of people who look like us are found there and are more than two hundred thousand years old. Starting perhaps sixty to seventy thousand years ago, groups of people spread out of Africa into Asia and Europe. They did not set out to explore. Each generation simply moved a little farther in search of game and plants, and over thousands of years they filled the land.

By about fifty thousand years ago people had reached Australia. That took boats, because even at Ice Age sea levels there were stretches of open ocean to cross. It is the oldest evidence we have of humans deliberately crossing the sea. In Europe, arriving humans met the Neanderthals, a different kind of human who had lived there for hundreds of thousands of years. The Neanderthals died out, but many people alive today carry a small share of Neanderthal ancestry.

The Americas were the last great landmass people reached. When the sea was low, a wide plain called *Beringia* connected Siberia to Alaska. Hunters following herds crossed it, and some may also have moved down the Pacific coast by boat. Archaeologists have found campsites in the Americas at least fourteen or fifteen thousand years old, and some argue for older ones. The details are still debated.

Everywhere they went, people adapted. In Australia, in the Arctic and on the American plains, they learned new plants, new animals and new dangers. By about twelve thousand years ago, humans lived on every continent except Antarctica. The hunter-gatherer way of life had spread across the whole planet. Almost nowhere yet did anyone farm.

words.d: the Ice Age land that connected Siberia and Alaska when the sea was low
the movement of people from one region to settle in another
an earlier kind of human who lived in Europe and western Asia and died out about forty thousand years ago

look.title: A Slow Journey
look.text: Suppose a band moves its camp only ten miles farther each generation, about every twenty-five years. Over a thousand years that is forty generations, or four hundred miles. Over ten thousand years it is four thousand miles.
look.prompt: Does this help explain how people could reach the far ends of the Earth without ever deciding to explore? What might speed the journey up or slow it down?

check.q: Where did modern humans first appear?
choices: Europe
Australia
The Americas
Africa
check.why: The oldest fossils of modern humans, more than two hundred thousand years old, come from Africa.

check.q: What does the settlement of Australia about fifty thousand years ago prove?
choices: People were already crossing open water in boats
Australia was connected to Africa by land
People reached Australia after the Americas
Neanderthals lived in Australia
check.why: Even at low sea levels, reaching Australia meant crossing open ocean, so people must have had boats.

check.q: How did people most likely first reach the Americas?
choices: By sailing across the Atlantic from Europe
By crossing Beringia from Siberia or moving down the Pacific coast
By walking north from Antarctica
By crossing a land bridge from Australia
check.why: When seas were low, Beringia joined Siberia and Alaska. People crossed it, and some may have followed the coast by boat.

lessons.title: Why Farming Began
lessons.mainIdea: Farming began about ten to eleven thousand years ago as a warming climate, growing populations and rich wild grain patches made settling down possible.
reading: For two hundred thousand years no one farmed. Then, within a few thousand years of the Ice Age ending, people in several parts of the world began to plant crops and keep animals. Historians call this the *Neolithic Revolution* or the farming revolution. It did not happen in a day. It was a slow shift that took many generations, and the people living through it did not know they were changing the world.

The earliest well-studied case is the *Fertile Crescent*, an arc of hills and river valleys that curves from what is now Israel and Lebanon through Syria and Turkey into Iraq and Iran. After the ice melted, this region grew warm and wet enough for huge stands of wild wheat and barley. People could harvest enough in a few weeks to last a year. So they stayed near the grain. Villages of stone-footed houses appeared there before any crops were planted.

Once people stayed in one place, planting made sense. A family could clear a patch, save the best seed, and sow it near home. Settled people also had more children, because babies did not have to be carried on long marches. More mouths meant more need for food, which meant more planting. By about ten thousand years ago, some of these villages depended on farmed wheat, barley, peas and lentils, along with herded goats and sheep.

One surprising site changed how scholars see this story. At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, hunter-gatherers built rings of carved stone pillars, some weighing many tons, around eleven and a half thousand years ago, before farming. Feeding the workers and gathering people for ceremonies may have pushed them toward growing grain. Perhaps people did not settle because they farmed. Perhaps they farmed because they had already begun to settle.

words.d: the slow shift from hunting and gathering to farming, starting about ten to eleven thousand years ago
an arc of rich land in the Middle East where some of the first farming began
extra food beyond what people need right away

look.title: Chicken or Egg
look.text: Old view: people learned to farm, and farming let them settle in villages. New view, based on sites like Göbekli Tepe: people settled first, for grain, for ceremonies, or for both, and settling pushed them to farm.
look.prompt: What kind of evidence would help you decide which came first, the village or the farm? What would you look for at a site?

check.q: Why did people in the Fertile Crescent begin to stay in one place before they farmed?
choices: Their kings ordered them to build cities
They had lost the skills of hunting
Thick stands of wild grain gave them a year's food in a few weeks
The ice sheets blocked every route out
check.why: Wild wheat and barley grew so thickly after the Ice Age that harvesting it could feed people for a year, so they stayed near it.

check.q: What did Göbekli Tepe show that surprised scholars?
choices: Farming began in the Americas
Cities existed before the Ice Age
People wrote before they farmed
Hunter-gatherers built huge stone monuments before farming
check.why: The stone pillar rings at Göbekli Tepe were built by people who did not yet farm, which suggests settling may have come before farming.

check.q: Why did settled people tend to have more children than mobile bands?
choices: Babies did not have to be carried on long marches
Settled people lived much longer
Wild animals could not reach villages
Farmers had doctors
check.why: Carrying babies limits how many young children a moving band can have. In a village that limit disappears.

lessons.title: Taming Plants and Animals
lessons.mainIdea: Domestication means changing plants and animals over generations by choosing which ones to breed, until they depend on people and people depend on them.
reading: Wild wheat drops its seeds the moment they ripen, so the plant can spread. That is bad for a harvester, because most seeds fall before they can be cut. A few wild plants carry a rare trait that makes seeds cling to the stalk. Every time people harvested with sickles, they collected more of the clinging seeds and fewer of the falling ones. When they planted those seeds, the next crop clung more. In a few centuries, wheat had changed into a plant that could not sow itself. It needed people.

This process is called *domestication*: changing a wild species over many generations by choosing which ones to breed. People domesticated wheat, barley, peas and lentils in the Fertile Crescent. They domesticated goats and sheep there too, choosing the calmest animals to keep and eating the wild-tempered ones. Over time the herds became smaller, tamer and woollier than their wild cousins. Cattle and pigs followed.

The first animal people domesticated was not for food. Dogs came from wolves, and they were living with hunter-gatherers thousands of years before any crop was planted. The oldest sure dog burials are more than fourteen thousand years old. Dogs helped hunt, guarded camps and ate scraps. Later, farmers added donkeys, horses, chickens and camels, each first tamed in a different part of the world.

Domestication changed people as much as it changed animals. Adults in most of the world cannot digest milk, but in places with a long history of dairy herding, most adults can. That ability spread because people who could drink milk had an extra food source. Farmers and their animals also began sharing diseases. Measles, flu and smallpox all likely came to people from herds. Living with animals was a bargain with a hidden price.

words.d: changing a wild plant or animal over generations by choosing which ones to breed, until it depends on people
to choose which animals or plants will produce the next generation
a feature of a living thing, such as seeds that cling to the stalk or a calm temper

look.title: Darwin on the Breeder's Hand
look.text: Charles Darwin argued that farmers and breeders had reshaped plants and animals simply by choosing, generation after generation, which ones to keep. The pigeon fancier, he wrote, could produce almost any form he wished by saving the birds that came closest to it. Nature, he said, did something similar over a far longer time.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication, 1868 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Darwin used domestic animals to help explain evolution. How is the way early farmers changed wheat like the way a pigeon breeder changes pigeons?

check.q: Why did domesticated wheat come to hold its seeds on the stalk?
choices: Farmers tied the seeds on by hand
People kept harvesting and replanting the clinging seeds, so that trait spread
Wild wheat always held its seeds
The warmer climate made seeds sticky
check.why: Harvesters collected more clinging seeds than falling ones. Planting them made each crop cling more, generation after generation.

check.q: Which animal was domesticated first, long before farming?
choices: The sheep
The horse
The dog
The chicken
check.why: Dogs came from wolves and lived with hunter-gatherers thousands of years before crops were planted.

check.q: What was a hidden cost of living closely with herd animals?
choices: Herds ate all the wild plants
People forgot how to hunt
Animals refused to give milk
Diseases like measles and flu passed from animals to people
check.why: Several serious human diseases likely began in farm herds and spread to the people who lived beside them.

lessons.title: Farming Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: Farming was invented separately in several parts of the world, each with its own crops and animals.
reading: The Fertile Crescent was not the only place farming began. It was invented on its own, by different people who never met, in at least six or seven parts of the world. Each place tamed the plants and animals that happened to grow there. That is why the world's diets are so different. Nobody carried farming from one continent to another; people figured it out again and again.

In China, people along the Yangtze River domesticated rice, and people along the Yellow River domesticated millet, a small hardy grain, about nine thousand years ago. They kept pigs and, later, chickens. In Mexico, farmers slowly turned a wild grass called teosinte, with a cob barely an inch long, into corn, or *maize*. They added beans and squash. In the Andes mountains of South America, people grew potatoes and kept llamas. In New Guinea, farmers grew taro and bananas. In Africa, sorghum, yams and African rice were tamed in different regions.

The Americas had far fewer animals to domesticate. There were no wild horses, cattle, sheep or pigs left after the Ice Age. So American farmers relied on plants, plus llamas, turkeys and dogs. That difference mattered for thousands of years. Without draft animals, there were no plows and no carts, and without herds, fewer of the diseases that Old World people slowly grew used to.

The map of early farming is also a map of where later civilizations rose. Sumer grew from Fertile Crescent wheat. The Shang dynasty grew from millet and rice. The Olmec and Maya grew from maize. The crops came first. In the next two chapters, every city you read about stood on a field that someone had learned to plant thousands of years before.

words.d: corn, domesticated in Mexico from a wild grass called teosinte
a small, hardy grain first farmed along the Yellow River in China
an animal such as an ox or horse that pulls a plow or cart

look.title: Where Farming Began
look.cite: standard estimates, rounded; dates are debated and keep changing with new finds
look.prompt: These places are thousands of miles apart. What does it suggest that farming appeared in all of them within a few thousand years of the Ice Age ending?

check.q: Which statement about the origin of farming is correct?
choices: It was invented separately in several parts of the world
It was invented once and carried everywhere by traders
It began only in China
It began in Europe and spread to Asia
check.why: People in the Fertile Crescent, China, Mexico, the Andes, New Guinea and Africa each worked out farming on their own.

check.q: What wild plant did Mexican farmers slowly turn into maize?
choices: Millet
Teosinte
Wild rice
Sorghum
check.why: Teosinte is a wild grass with a tiny cob. Over thousands of years of selection it became corn.

check.q: Why did farmers in the Americas have no plows or carts for thousands of years?
choices: They did not know how to make wheels
Their crops did not need plowing

check.why: After the Ice Age the Americas had no wild horses, cattle or oxen to tame, so there were no draft animals for pulling.

sections.title: Villages and New Ways of Life

lessons.title: Surplus, Storage and Specialists
lessons.mainIdea: When farmers grew more than they could eat, some people could stop farming and become specialists, and societies began to divide into classes.
reading: A good harvest gives a farming family more grain than it can eat. That extra is a *surplus*. Hunter-gatherers rarely had one, because wild food spoils and cannot be carried. Farmers could store grain in pits, jars and mud-brick rooms for years. A surplus is more than a full stomach. It is time. If ten families grow enough for twelve, two families can do something else.

That something else is *specialization*. In a farming village, one person might spend the whole year making pottery, another chipping obsidian blades, another weaving cloth. Specialists got better at their craft than anyone in a band could, and they traded their goods for food. Pottery itself was a farming invention: hunters do not haul clay jars around, but villagers needed them to store grain and cook porridge.

Surplus also created something new: inequality. In a band, no one could pile up much more than anyone else. In a village, a family with the best land and a full storeroom could feed workers, buy goods and pass its wealth to its children. Over centuries, some families became richer than others, and *social classes* appeared: people ranked by wealth and power. Archaeologists see the beginning of this in graves. In the oldest villages, everyone is buried much the same. In later ones, a few people are buried with jewelry, weapons and fine pottery, and most are buried with nothing.

Someone also had to guard the grain, settle fights over land and decide when to plant. Leaders gained power because they controlled the surplus. Priests explained the weather and the harvest. Warriors defended the storerooms or raided the neighbors'. The small, mostly equal band was turning into something with a top and a bottom.

words.d: extra food beyond what people need right away
when a person does one kind of work full time, such as making pots, instead of producing all their own food
a group of people ranked together by wealth, power or the work they do

look.title: Two Cemeteries
look.text: In an early village cemetery, forty graves each hold a body, a few beads and a simple pot. In a later cemetery nearby, one grave holds a man with a copper dagger, a polished stone axe, hundreds of beads and three fine bowls. The other thirty-nine graves hold almost nothing.
look.prompt: What changed between the two cemeteries? What do the graves tell you that no written record could?

check.q: What is a surplus?
choices: The land a family farms
Extra food beyond what people need right away
A tax paid to a leader
A tool for cutting grain
check.why: A surplus is the extra a good harvest leaves over. It can be stored and used to feed people who are not farming.

check.q: How did a surplus make specialization possible?
choices: Everyone had to work harder in the fields
Surplus grain was used as money
If some families grew enough for everyone, others could spend their time on crafts
Specialists could not eat grain
check.why: When farmers grew more than they needed, other people could make pots, blades or cloth full time and trade for food.

check.q: How do archaeologists see the beginning of social classes?
choices: In written laws about rank
In the size of each village's fields
In paintings of kings
In graves where a few people are buried with far more than everyone else
check.why: Equal graves show an equal society. When a few graves are packed with wealth and most hold nothing, classes have appeared.

lessons.title: Çatalhöyük: A Town Without Streets
lessons.mainIdea: Çatalhöyük in Turkey was one of the largest early farming settlements, a packed town of mud-brick houses entered through the roof.
reading: About nine thousand years ago, on a plain in what is now central Turkey, several thousand people lived in a single dense settlement. Archaeologists call it *Çatalhöyük*, a Turkish name meaning fork mound. It was not a city with temples, palaces or streets. It was a honeycomb of mud-brick houses built wall to wall, so tightly that there were no roads at all. People walked across the rooftops and climbed down ladders into their homes through a hole in the ceiling that also let out smoke from the hearth.

Inside, the walls were plastered white and repainted often, sometimes with pictures of hunts, geometric patterns, vultures and what may be a map of the town below an erupting volcano. Some houses had the horns of wild bulls set into the walls. People buried their dead under the floors of their own houses, sometimes many bodies in one home, and kept living on top of them. When a house grew old, they filled it in and built a new one on the same spot, layer on layer, until the mound rose above the plain.

The people of Çatalhöyük farmed wheat, barley and peas and kept sheep and goats, but they still hunted wild cattle and gathered wild plants. They traded obsidian, a black volcanic glass that makes razor-sharp blades, from mountains far away. They made pottery, baskets, wooden bowls, and small clay figures of animals and heavy-bodied people. There is no sign of a ruler's house, a temple or a wall. Most houses are about the same size.

The site was first dug by the British archaeologist James Mellaart in the early 1960s and by a large international team starting in the 1990s. Their careful work shows a town that was big and crowded but, as far as we can tell, still fairly equal. Çatalhöyük is a snapshot of the moment after farming and before kings.

words.d: a large farming settlement in Turkey about nine thousand years ago, with houses entered through the roof
black volcanic glass that can be chipped into extremely sharp blades
a building block of clay and straw dried hard in the sun

look.title: The Excavator's Report
look.text: James Mellaart reported that the houses were entered from the roof by a ladder, that the rooms had raised platforms for sitting and sleeping, that the dead lay beneath these platforms, and that the walls carried paintings and plaster reliefs unlike anything then known from so early a date.
look.cite: James Mellaart, reports on the Çatalhöyük excavations, 1960s (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Mellaart could describe what he found but had to guess what it meant. Pick one detail here and give two different explanations for it.

check.q: How did people enter their houses at Çatalhöyük?
choices: Through the roof, by ladder
Through doors on a main street
Through tunnels underground
Through gates in the town wall
check.why: The houses were built wall to wall with no streets. People crossed the roofs and climbed down ladders through a hole in the ceiling.

check.q: What evidence suggests Çatalhöyük was still a fairly equal society?
choices: Everyone was buried in a single royal tomb
Most houses were about the same size, with no palace or temple
The town had a strong wall and an army
The people did not farm
check.why: Without a ruler's house or temple, and with houses of similar size, there is no sign of a wealthy ruling class.

check.q: Why is obsidian at Çatalhöyük important evidence?
choices: It proves the people were miners
It shows they used iron tools
It shows they traded with distant places
It shows they had no pottery
check.why: Obsidian came from volcanic mountains far away, so its presence shows trade or travel over long distances.

lessons.title: Was Farming Worth It?
lessons.mainIdea: Farming let human numbers grow and made civilization possible, but the first farmers were often less healthy, less free and harder working than the hunters they replaced.
reading: It is easy to assume farming was simply progress. It fed more people, which is why farmers eventually outnumbered hunter-gatherers almost everywhere. It made villages, then cities, then writing, law and everything else in this course. But archaeologists who study skeletons have found something uncomfortable. In many regions, the first farmers were shorter than the hunter-gatherers before them, had more cavities from a starchy diet, and showed more signs of childhood hunger and disease.

Farmers ate a narrower diet, mostly one or two grains, so a bad harvest meant *famine*, a season of hunger that a band could have walked away from. Farmers worked longer hours: clearing, plowing, weeding, harvesting, grinding. Their bent spines and worn knees show it. Living packed together with animals and their own waste, they suffered from new diseases. And once a family had fields and a storeroom, it could not leave, which made it easier to tax, rule and raid.

So why did farming win? Because it works at the level of populations, not individuals. A farming village could feed ten times as many people on the same land as a band of foragers. More people meant more soldiers, more workers and more children to inherit the fields. Hunter-gatherers were pushed to the margins, or joined the farmers, or were overrun. It did not matter that each farmer might have been worse off than each hunter.

Some scholars have called farming the worst mistake in human history. Others point out that without it there would be no music halls, no hospitals and no books. Both sides are reading the same bones and the same storerooms. The question you should carry into the next chapters is this: when a change makes a whole society stronger but many of its people worse off, who gets to decide whether it was worth it?

words.d: a time of severe hunger when crops fail and food runs out
the number of people living in a place

look.title: Hours of Work for Food
look.unit: hours per adult per week, rough
look.cite: rough figures from anthropological studies and historical estimates; actual numbers vary widely by place and season
look.prompt: If these rough numbers are close to right, why would anyone choose the harder life? Think about what farming gave in return for the extra hours.

check.q: What do skeletons tell us about many early farmers compared with hunter-gatherers?
choices: Farmers were taller and had fewer cavities
Farmers had no diseases at all
There is no way to compare them
Farmers were often shorter, with more cavities and signs of hunger
check.why: Bones and teeth show a narrower, starchier diet and harder work among many early farming groups.

check.q: Why did farming societies spread even if each farmer was often worse off?
choices: Farming fed far more people on the same land, so farmers outnumbered foragers
Hunter-gatherers voted to become farmers
Farming was easier work than hunting
Foragers could not have children
check.why: A farming village could support many times more people than a band, and larger numbers won out over time.

check.q: Why was a farmer easier to tax or rule than a hunter-gatherer?
choices: Farmers were less intelligent
Farmers could not leave their fields and stored grain behind
Hunter-gatherers had stronger weapons
Farmers wanted to be ruled
check.why: A band could walk away from a bully. A family with fields and a full storeroom was tied to one place.

review.q: Which of these is the best source of evidence about people who lived before writing?
choices: Tools, bones and remains dug from sites
Letters written by ancient kings
Modern novels about cave people
Maps drawn in the Middle Ages
review.why: Prehistory has no written records, so archaeologists rely on the physical remains people left behind.

review.q: Deeper layers of soil are usually older. What is this rule called?
choices: Domestication
Stratigraphy
Migration
Specialization
review.why: Stratigraphy is reading the layers of the ground, with deeper layers laid down earlier.

review.q: Which best describes how hunter-gatherer bands were led?
choices: By kings who inherited their power
By priests who owned all the land
By people others chose to listen to, who could be ignored
By elected councils with written laws
review.why: Bands had no kings or ranks. Leaders were respected people, and anyone who bossed others could simply be ignored.

review.q: What happened to the giant Ice Age animals such as mammoths when the world warmed?
choices: They moved to the Fertile Crescent
They were domesticated by farmers
They grew larger
Most died out, from climate change, hunting or both
review.why: As the ice melted and forests spread, and as hunters pressed them, most of the giant animals became extinct.

review.q: In which region did people first farm wheat, barley, goats and sheep?
choices: The Fertile Crescent
The Andes
New Guinea
The Yellow River valley
review.why: Wheat, barley, goats and sheep were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent about ten to eleven thousand years ago.

review.q: A wild plant whose seeds cling to the stalk instead of falling has an advantage under which condition?
choices: When it must spread itself without people
When people are harvesting with sickles and replanting the seed
When the climate is very cold
When goats graze on it
review.why: Clinging seeds are collected and replanted by harvesters, so the trait spreads under farming even though it hurts a wild plant.

review.q: What made Çatalhöyük unusual compared with a modern town?
choices: It had huge temples and a palace
It was built entirely of stone
It had no streets; people walked on the roofs and entered by ladder
It was surrounded by a moat
review.why: The mud-brick houses were built wall to wall with no roads between them. Roofs served as the town's paths.

review.q: Which is the strongest argument that farming was not simply good for people?
choices: Farmers had more children than foragers
Farming let cities and writing develop
Farming villages grew larger than bands
Skeletons of early farmers show poorer health and harder work
review.why: The bone evidence points to a real cost to individuals, even as farming made societies larger and stronger.
